Project ALS — Natural Language Database Access

Benchmarking Local LLMs for Genomic Data Querying

Projecticum Data Science

May 11, 2026

1. Project Background

What is Project MinE?

Project MinE is an international collaboration coordinated by the research group of Kevin Kenna at UMC Utrecht, involving 27 centers across 21 countries. The project sequences the genomes of ALS patients to map genetic variants associated with the disease.

The genetic data is stored in VCF format inside an SQL database. Accessing this database currently requires:

  • Proficiency in SQL querying
  • Knowledge of VCF format and genomic annotation
  • Familiarity with the R package rvat

This creates a significant barrier for researchers who are not bioinformaticians.

The Goal

Make the database accessible to a wider group of scientists using natural language processing — allowing researchers to query the database in plain English, without writing a single line of SQL.

2. Pipeline Architecture

Technology Stack

The pipeline is built from three core components:

Component Role
rvat R package by Kenna Lab — opens and manages the .gdb genomic database
querychat R package by Posit — converts natural language → SQL queries
rollama / ollama Runs a local LLM to power the NLP

How It Works

The user types a plain English question. The local LLM interprets the intent and generates an SQL query via querychat. The query is executed against the database and the results are returned as a natural language answer.

Current querychat pipeline

Example Query

library(ellmer)
library(querychat)
library(rvat)
library(DBI)

# Connect to the ALS genomic database
gdb <- gdb(rvat_example("rvatData.gdb"))

# Set up the chat client with a local LLM
ollama_client <- chat_ollama(
  model  = "llama3.1:8b",
  params = ellmer::params(temperature = 0.1, num_predict = 200)
)

# Initialise QueryChat
qc <- QueryChat$new(
  data_source      = gdb,
  table_name       = "varInfo_synthetic",
  client           = ollama_client,
  data_description = data_description,
  extra_instructions = extra_instructions
)

# Launch interactive console
qc$console()

3. The Database

Structure

The varInfo_synthetic table used for benchmarking contains 1802 variants with the following key columns:

Column Description
VAR_id Unique variant identifier
CHROM Chromosome (e.g. chr1)
POS Genomic position
gene_name Gene the variant falls in
HighImpact 1 = high impact (stop-gain, frameshift); 0 otherwise
ModerateImpact 1 = moderate impact (missense); 0 otherwise
Synonymous 1 = synonymous (silent); 0 otherwise
CADDphred Deleteriousness score; higher = more deleterious; missing = ‘.’
PolyPhen D=probably damaging, P=possibly damaging, B=benign; missing = ‘.’
SIFT D=deleterious, T=tolerated; missing = ‘.’
ALS_1–ALS_5 Genotype of 5 ALS patients (0=hom ref, 1=het, 2=hom alt)
Control_1–Control_5 Genotype of 5 controls (same encoding)

Important Data Rules

  • A variant cannot be both Synonymous and HighImpact simultaneously
  • Missing values in CADDphred, PolyPhen, and SIFT are stored as '.' — not NULL
  • PolyPhen and SIFT are computational predictions only — not evidence of pathogenicity
  • Genotype values indicate zygosity only — not disease association

4. Benchmark Design

Question Categories

The benchmark was designed to test three types of queries:

Category Description Example
Lookup (L1–L5) Simple filtering and counting queries — e.g. ‘How many variants are in NEK1?’ How many variants in TARDBP are predicted deleterious by SIFT?
Analytical (A1–A5) Aggregations and calculations — e.g. ‘What is the total allele burden in cases vs controls?’ What is the average allele frequency for synonymous, moderate, and high-impact variants separately?
Unanswerable (U1–U5) Questions the database cannot answer — tests hallucination avoidance What is the average age of ALS cases?

Grading Criteria

Each response was graded on 4 criteria (pass/fail), giving a maximum score of 4 per question:

Criterion What it tests
grade_answer Is the final answer correct or appropriate?
grade_minimal_response Is the response concise (1–3 sentences)?
grade_hallucination Is the response free of hallucinations?
grade_sql Is the SQL query logically correct?

Evaluation Methodology

The benchmark was run 3 times per model to account for variability. Responses were first auto-graded using a local LLM judge (gemma3) with the full benchmark document as ground truth, then manually reviewed for any rows the auto-grader could not parse.

5. Models Tested

Model Size Notes
llama3.1:8b 4.9 GB Preferred by research group; good tool calling
llama3.2 2.0 GB Lighter version of llama3; faster but less capable
mistral 4.4 GB Strong instruction following; weaker tool calling
qwen3:8b 5.2 GB Strong reasoning; good structured output
deepseek-r1:8b 5.2 GB Reasoning-focused; failed tool calling entirely

All models were run locally via Ollama on the Posit Workbench server — no external API calls, no data leaving the server.

7. Key Findings

What Worked Well

  • SQL generation was generally correct across all models that executed tool calls — the LLMs understood the schema and wrote valid queries
  • Unanswerable questions were handled better than expected — most models correctly refused questions about missing columns (age, population-specific AF, pathogenicity)
  • llama3.1:8b showed the lowest hallucination rate, consistent with the research group’s prior experience
  • The pipeline is fully local — no data leaves the server, which is critical for sensitive genomic data

What Needs Improvement

  • Response verbosity — all models struggled with conciseness, often returning long rambling responses instead of a direct 1–3 sentence answer
  • Instruction following — smaller local models consistently ignored formatting rules despite explicit instructions in the system prompt
  • Mistral’s tool calling — Mistral scored highest overall but does not actually execute queries; it writes SQL as text without running it, making it unsuitable for this pipeline despite good scores
  • Ambiguous questions — models rarely asked for clarification when terms like “most important” were used

The Mistral Paradox

Mistral achieved the highest benchmark score (2.69/4) but is the least suitable model for production use, as it does not call the querychat tool and therefore never actually queries the database. llama3.1:8b, preferred by the research group, scores lower (2.36/4) but correctly executes the full pipeline.

This highlights an important limitation of automated benchmarking — scores do not always reflect real-world usefulness.

8. Limitations

  • The benchmark was run on a synthetic dataset — specific values differ from the real Project MinE database, so only SQL logic correctness (not exact values) was fully verifiable
  • Only 5 ALS patients and 5 controls were included in the synthetic data — real analyses involve thousands of samples
  • The auto-grader (gemma3) introduced some inconsistency — approximately 10–15% of rows required manual review
  • All models were tested with identical prompts — further prompt engineering per model might improve individual performance

9. Future Work — MCP Agent

Why querychat Has Limitations

The current querychat pipeline is limited to one input table at a time. Real genomic analyses often require:

  • Joining variant data with phenotype data (pheno table)
  • Running RVAT association tests
  • Querying multiple tables simultaneously

The Proposed Solution: MCP Agent

The next phase of the project involves building a Model Context Protocol (MCP) agent in Python that can:

  • Expose multiple data sources as separate tools the LLM can call
  • Integrate RVAT functions as callable tools (not just SQL)
  • Handle multi-step reasoning across tables
  • Give full control over response formatting

Why MCP Over querychat?

querychat MCP Agent
Multiple data sources ✗ ✓
RVAT integration ✗ ✓
Response formatting control Limited Full
Extensibility Limited High
Setup complexity Low Medium

9b. Alternative Approaches — Extending querychat

Before committing to the full MCP agent architecture, two lighter-weight alternatives are worth exploring. Both stay entirely within R, avoiding the added complexity of a Python backend and an HTTP layer between Shiny and the agent.

Approach 1 — Forking querychat

How querychat works internally

querychat is relatively thin. At its core it does three things:

  1. Builds a system prompt describing the target tables schema and any extra instructions
  2. Passes the users question + that system prompt to an ellmer chat client
  3. Executes the returned SQL against the database and returns the result

The key entry point is QueryChat$new(), which accepts a single table_name and builds its schema description from that one table. The multi-table limitation is therefore not architectural — it is simply a consequence of how the system prompt is constructed.

The workaround

By forking the querychat source and modifying the schema-building step, it should be possible to:

  • Accept a list of tables (e.g. varInfo, pheno) instead of a single table_name
  • Describe all table schemas and their relationships in the system prompt (primary keys, how tables join)
  • Allow the LLM to generate multi-table SQL (JOIN queries) rather than single-table queries

The rest of the pipeline — the ellmer chat client, the SQL execution step, the Shiny integration — would remain unchanged.

What needs investigating

  • Where exactly in the querychat source is the system prompt constructed? Which function or R6 method handles schema introspection?
  • Does querychat validate or sanitise the returned SQL before executing it? Would JOIN queries pass through unmodified?
  • Are there any hardcoded assumptions about a single table elsewhere in the codebase (e.g. in how results are returned or displayed)?
  • How does querychat handle execution errors — would a malformed JOIN cause a silent failure or a visible error?

Relevant source to look at

# Install the development version to inspect source
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("posit-dev/querychat")

# Browse the R6 class definition
querychat:::QueryChat

Approach 2 — Using ellmer directly

What this means

Since querychat is itself a wrapper around ellmer, it is possible to bypass querychat entirely and use ellmers tool-calling interface directly. This gives full control over:

  • How many tables are described in the system prompt
  • What tools the LLM can call (SQL queries, RVAT functions, metadata lookups)
  • How responses are formatted before being returned to Shiny

The tradeoff is that you are rebuilding what querychat already provides — SQL execution, result handling, conversation history — from scratch in R.

Sketch of the approach

library(ellmer)
library(DBI)
library(rvat)

# Connect to database
gdb <- gdb(rvat_example("rvatData.gdb"))

# Define a SQL execution tool the LLM can call
run_sql <- function(query) {
  tryCatch(
    dbGetQuery(gdb@db, query),
    error = function(e) paste("SQL error:", e$message)
  )
}

# Define an RVAT tool the LLM can call
run_rvat_burden <- function(gene, group_col = "ALS_status") {
  # placeholder — actual rvat call goes here
  paste("RVAT burden test for", gene, "not yet implemented")
}

# Build a system prompt describing all available tables and tools
system_prompt <- "
You are a genomic data assistant with access to two tools:
  - run_sql: executes a SQL query against the variant database
  - run_rvat_burden: runs a rare variant burden test for a given gene

The database contains the following tables:

varInfo columns: VAR_id, CHROM, POS, gene_name, HighImpact, ModerateImpact,
Synonymous, CADDphred, PolyPhen, SIFT, ALS_1 through ALS_5, Control_1 
through Control_5.

pheno columns: sample_id, ALS_status, age_at_onset, site_of_onset, sex.

varInfo and pheno share no direct join key in SQL — use RVAT for 
case/control analyses that require both tables.

Always respond in 1-3 sentences. Do not hallucinate columns that are not listed.
"

# Initialise ellmer chat with tool definitions
client <- chat_ollama(
  model  = "llama3.1:8b",
  system = system_prompt,
  params = ellmer::params(temperature = 0.1)
)

# Register tools
client$register_tool(tool(
  run_sql,
  "Execute a SQL query against the genomic variant database.",
  query = type_string("A valid SQLite query.")
))

client$register_tool(tool(
  run_rvat_burden,
  "Run a rare variant burden test for a given gene using RVAT.",
  gene     = type_string("The gene name to test."),
  group_col = type_string("Column to use for case/control grouping.")
))

# Ask a question
client$chat("How many high-impact variants are in NEK1?")

What needs investigating

  • Does ellmer support registering multiple tools and does llama3.1:8b reliably select between them? Tool selection failures were already observed with some models in the benchmark.
  • What is the correct ellmer syntax for register_tool and tool() in the current version — the API has been evolving and documentation is sparse.
  • How does conversation history work in ellmer when tool calls are involved — does it automatically maintain context across multi-turn queries?
  • Can the Shiny integration from the current querychat app be adapted to work with a raw ellmer client, or does it depend on querychat-specific internals?

Comparison of approaches

Fork querychat ellmer directly MCP Agent
Multi-table SQL ✓ (with modification) ✓ ✓
RVAT integration ✗ (SQL only) ✓ ✓
Stays in R ✓ ✓ ✗
Shiny compatibility ✓ (minimal changes) Needs testing Needs HTTP layer
Implementation effort Low–medium Medium High
Modifies upstream package Yes No No

The fork approach is the quickest path to multi-table SQL. The ellmer approach is more powerful and avoids dependency on querychats internals, but requires more groundwork. Both are worth prototyping before deciding whether the full MCP architecture is necessary.

9c. Implementation — MultiTableSource

Approach

Rather than forking the querychat package or rebuilding the pipeline in Python, the multi-table limitation was resolved by implementing querychat’s existing DataSource interface directly. This required no changes to the querychat source code and no new dependencies — everything stays within R.

The entry point was normalize_data_source(), which contains an early exit:

if (is_data_source(data_source)) {
    return(data_source)
}

Where is_data_source() simply checks:

inherits(x, "DataSource")

This means any R6 class inheriting from querychat:::DataSource is accepted as-is, bypassing all single-table wrapping logic. The interface required is five methods: get_schema(), execute_query(), test_query(), get_data(), and get_db_type().

What Was Built

MultiTableSource is a ~60 line R6 class that:

  • Accepts a DBIConnection and a vector of table names instead of a single table
  • Overrides get_schema() to call querychat’s internal get_schema_impl() once per table and concatenate the results — this is what gets injected into the LLM system prompt
  • Treats the first table as the primary display table for get_data() and test_query(require_all_columns = TRUE)
  • Delegates execute_query() and test_query() directly to DBI

One additional change was required: the default querychat prompt template contains the line "For security reasons, you may only query this specific table." This is hardcoded outside any conditional block and would cause the LLM to ignore the second table despite it being present in the schema. The fix was to copy the template, replace that line with "You may query any of the tables described in the schema above.", and pass the custom template path via the prompt_template argument to QueryChat$new().

Two minor errors were encountered during setup:

  • gdb@db is not a valid slot — the gdb object itself is the DBIConnection and should be passed directly
  • QueryChat$new() attempts to build an id string via sprintf("querychat_%s", table_name), which fails when table_name is a vector; resolved by passing id = "querychat_multi" explicitly

Results

The implementation was tested against three questions:

Question Table queried Result
What is the average age of ALS cases? pheno 60.1 years — correct
What is the sex distribution of the cohort? pheno 51.6% / 48.4% — correct
How many high-impact variants are in SOD1? varInfo_synthetic 4 — incorrect

The LLM correctly routed each query to the appropriate table without any explicit routing logic — schema description alone was sufficient. All previously unanswerable benchmark questions involving sample metadata (age, sex, population) are now answerable.

What This Means for the Benchmark

Several questions graded as unanswerable in the original benchmark — and correctly refused by the models — are now answerable with this implementation. The benchmark results therefore represent a lower bound on what the pipeline can achieve; a re-run with MultiTableSource would be needed to assess performance on pheno-level questions.

Limitations

  • The pheno table has a column also named pheno (1 = ALS case, 0 = control), which is potentially ambiguous for the LLM. This should be clarified in data_description.
  • Dashboard filtering (querychat_update_dashboard) still operates on the primary table only (varInfo_synthetic) — filtered views of the pheno table are not supported in the current implementation.
  • The two tables are not directly joinable via a shared column value. IID values in pheno (e.g. ALS1) correspond to column names in varInfo_synthetic (e.g. ALS_1), not column values — cross-table analyses therefore cannot be expressed as a single SQL JOIN.

10. Shiny Application

What is Shiny?

Shiny is an R framework for building interactive web applications directly from R code — no HTML, CSS, or JavaScript required. In the context of this project, Shiny provides the graphical user interface that researchers interact with, sitting on top of the querychat pipeline.

Instead of typing queries in an R console, users get a clean web interface with a chat sidebar and a live data table — making the tool accessible to non-technical researchers.

Basic Shiny Structure

The Shiny app wrapping our QueryChat pipeline looks like this:

library(shiny)
library(bslib)
library(shinycssloaders)
library(DT)

library(querychat)
library(rvat)
library(ellmer)

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# DATABASE
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────

gdb_conn <- gdb(rvat_example("rvatData.gdb"))

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# LOCAL LLM
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────

client <- chat_ollama(
  model = "llama3.1:8b",
  params = ellmer::params(
    temperature = 0.1,
    num_predict = 200
  )
)

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# QUERYCHAT
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────

qc <- QueryChat$new(
  data_source = gdb_conn,
  table_name = "varInfo_synthetic",
  client = client
)

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# UI
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────

ui <- page_sidebar(
  
  title = "Project ALS",
  
  theme = bs_theme(
    version = 5,
    bootswatch = "flatly"
  ),
  
  sidebar = sidebar(
    
    width = 350,
    
    h4("Ask a Question"),
    
    textAreaInput(
      inputId = "question",
      label = NULL,
      placeholder = "Example:\nHow many high-impact variants are in SOD1?",
      rows = 5
    ),
    
    actionButton("submit", "Run Query", class = "btn-primary"),
    br(), br(),
    actionButton("reset_chat", "Reset Conversation", class = "btn-danger"),
    
    hr(),
    
    h5("Example Questions"),
    tags$ul(
      tags$li("How many variants are in NEK1?"),
      tags$li("Show all high-impact variants"),
      tags$li("Which gene contains the most variants?"),
      tags$li("How many variants are predicted deleterious by SIFT?")
    )
  ),
  
  layout_columns(
    
    col_widths = c(5, 7),
    
    card(
      full_screen = TRUE,
      card_header(h4("Chat")),
      
      div(
        style = "height:700px; overflow-y:auto; padding:15px; background:#f8f9fa;",
        shinycssloaders::withSpinner(uiOutput("chat_history"))
      )
    ),
    
    card(
      full_screen = TRUE,
      card_header(h4("Debug Information")),
      
      h5("Available QueryChat methods"),
      verbatimTextOutput("methods_output"),
      
      h5("Last response"),
      verbatimTextOutput("raw_response")
    )
  )
)

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# SERVER
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  
  rv <- reactiveValues(messages = list(), raw_response = NULL)
  
  # Methods debug
  output$methods_output <- renderPrint({
    names(qc)
  })
  
  # RUN QUERY
  observeEvent(input$submit, {
    
    req(input$question)
    
    response <- tryCatch(
      {
        # ✅ FIX: correct QueryChat call
        qc$ui$chat(input$question)
      },
      error = function(e) {
        paste("ERROR:", e$message)
      }
    )
    
    rv$raw_response <- response
    
    rv$messages <- append(rv$messages, list(
      list(
        question = input$question,
        answer = paste(response, collapse = "\n")
      )
    ))
    
    updateTextAreaInput(session, "question", value = "")
  })
  
  # RESET
  observeEvent(input$reset_chat, {
    rv$messages <- list()
    rv$raw_response <- NULL
  })
  
  # CHAT OUTPUT
  output$chat_history <- renderUI({
    
    if (length(rv$messages) == 0) {
      return(
        div(
          style = "text-align:center; margin-top:50px; color:grey;",
          h4("No conversation yet"),
          p("Ask a question to begin.")
        )
      )
    }
    
    tagList(
      lapply(rv$messages, function(msg) {
        
        div(
          style = "margin-bottom:25px;",
          
          div(
            style = "background:#457B9D; color:white; padding:12px; border-radius:12px; margin-bottom:10px;",
            tags$b("You"), br(), msg$question
          ),
          
          div(
            style = "background:white; border:1px solid #dee2e6; padding:12px; border-radius:12px;",
            tags$b("Assistant"), br(), msg$answer
          )
        )
      })
    )
  })
  
  # RAW OUTPUT
  output$raw_response <- renderPrint({
    rv$raw_response
  })
}

shinyApp(ui, server)

11. Proposed Production Architecture

Combining the MCP agent backend with the Shiny frontend, the full proposed production pipeline would look as follows:

Proposed production architecture

Why This Architecture?

Layer Role Why this choice
Shiny (R) User-facing interface — chat sidebar, results table, SQL display Native R integration, familiar to the research group, querychat-compatible
MCP Agent (Python) Orchestrates tool calls, manages context, routes requests MCP is purpose-built for multi-tool LLM orchestration
Ollama / Llama 3.1 Understands natural language, decides which tools to call Local model — no data leaves the server, free to run
Tools Execute queries, run RVAT analyses, retrieve metadata Separating tools means new data sources can be added without rebuilding the pipeline

12. Conclusions

The proof-of-concept demonstrates that local LLMs can successfully translate natural language queries into SQL for genomic variant databases. The pipeline is:

  • Functional — queries execute correctly for most question types
  • Private — fully local, no external API calls
  • Accessible — researchers without SQL knowledge can retrieve data

However, the current implementation has clear limitations that motivate the move to an MCP agent architecture for the production version.

Recommended model for current pipeline: llama3.1:8b — lowest hallucination rate, correct tool calling, consistent with research group preference.

This document was generated as part of the Projecticum Data Science course. All genomic data used in benchmarking is synthetic.
